Fighting game series.Soulcalibur: A weapons-based fighter from Namco, and a sequel to Soul Edge; its Dreamcast version was a showcase for that console's graphics.
Fighting game series.The King of Fighters: SNK's team-based fighter, which began in 1994 and brings characters from its other games, such as Fatal Fury, together.
Fighting game series.Dead or Alive: Tecmo's series is known for fast counters and its bouncy physics, and was a hit on the original Xbox.
Fighting game series.Virtua Fighter: Sega's 1993 arcade game was the first 3D polygon fighter, and its blocky characters set the stage for Tekken and Soulcalibur.
Fighting game series.Killer Instinct: A 1994 arcade fighter famed for long combo chains, whose comeback on Xbox One in 2013 was made by Double Helix.
Fighting game series.Guilty Gear: Arc System Works' anime-styled series is known for fast play and a heavy metal soundtrack, with song titles drawn from rock bands.
Fighting game series.Bloody Roar: A fighting series where characters turn into beasts mid-fight, its idea resting on a mix of human and animal forms.
Fighting game series.Halo: A sci-fi shooter, so combat is guns, not fists.
Fighting game series.Doom: A shooter, not a fighting game; its combat is with shotguns and demons.
Fighting game series.Zelda: An adventure series; Link fights monsters, but not in structured one-on-one matches.
Fighting game series.Tetris: A puzzle game, so any competing is about stacking blocks, not fighting.
Fighting game series.Pac-Man: A maze chase from 1980, which has a ghosts-and-dots battle, but not hand-to-hand combat.
Fighting game series.FIFA: A soccer series, whose competition happens on a pitch and not in a ring.
Fighting game series.Madden NFL: A football simulation; players tackle, but it's a sports game rather than a fighting one.
Fighting game series.Minecraft: A sandbox building game, not a fighter, even if you can battle mobs.
Fighting game series.Mario Kart: A racing series, where you throw shells, but it is not a fighting series.
Fighting game series.Pokemon: Creatures battle, but in turn-based RPG fashion, not in a real-time fighting game.
Fighting game series.Sonic: A platformer, and the speedy hedgehog spin-attacks, but it isn't a fighter, though he appears in Smash.
Fighting game series.Gran Turismo: A driving simulator that focuses on real cars; no fighting involved.
Fighting game series.Final Fantasy: A role-playing series with fights, but in menu-driven battles rather than a fighting game.

Things in a medicine cabinet.Aspirin: Aspirin comes from willow bark, a remedy used for thousands of years, and Bayer made the synthetic version in 1899.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Plasters: The adhesive bandage was invented in 1920 by Earle Dickson, a cotton buyer, to help his accident-prone wife.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Thermometer: Mercury thermometers have mostly been replaced by digital ones, since mercury is toxic if the glass breaks.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Cough syrup: Many cough syrups were once made with opium or alcohol, and they're now far more tightly regulated.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Tweezers: Tweezers have been used for thousands of years, with bronze ones found in ancient Egyptian and Roman sites.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Antacids: Antacids work by neutralizing stomach acid, usually with calcium carbonate, which is also chalk.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Cotton swabs: Cotton swabs are best kept out of your ears, since pushing them in can pack wax or damage the eardrum.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Nail clippers: Nail clippers use a lever to multiply force, and the modern design was patented in the late 1800s.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Allergy pills: Antihistamine pills block histamine, the chemical your body releases that makes you sneeze and itch.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Eye drops: Eye drops have to be sterile, since the eye is sensitive, and bottles are discarded within a month of opening.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Antiseptic cream: Joseph Lister pioneered antiseptic surgery in the 1860s by using carbolic acid to clean wounds.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Ibuprofen: Ibuprofen was discovered in the 1960s by a British team, and it reduces inflammation as well as pain.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Butter: Butter belongs in the fridge or on the table, and it's not a medicine, though old folk remedies used it on burns.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Ketchup: In the 1830s, ketchup was sold as a medicine for indigestion, and the cure turned into a condiment.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Spatula: A spatula lives in the kitchen drawer, and it's not a medical instrument.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Stapler: A stapler fastens paper and lives on a desk, and it's an office tool rather than a medical one.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Hammer: A hammer lives in the toolbox, and the medical 'reflex hammer' used by doctors is a different thing.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Teabags: Teabags live in the kitchen cupboard, and they were invented by accident in 1908 when a tea merchant sent samples in silk bags.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Cereal: Cornflakes were invented by John Harvey Kellogg in the 1890s as a healthy food for patients at his sanitarium.
Things in a medicine cabinet.TV remote: A TV remote lives in the living room, and it's one of the most germ-covered objects in a house.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Socks: Socks go in the dresser, though Roman soldiers wore early forms of them under their sandals.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Light bulb: Bulbs live in a drawer or cupboard, and you'd normally store them away from the bathroom.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Garden gloves: Garden gloves stay in the shed, away from the medicine, and they protect hands from thorns.
Things in a medicine cabinet.Doorknob: A doorknob is fixed to a door, and it's a classic germ spot that rarely sits in a cabinet.

Things you set a dinner table with.Plate: Dinner plates have grown over the decades, and the average size today is much larger than a century ago.
Things you set a dinner table with.Fork: In formal settings, the forks are laid out in order of use, from the outside in.
Things you set a dinner table with.Dinner knife: The blade of a place-setting knife faces the plate, a custom said to date back to avoiding any hint of threat.
Things you set a dinner table with.Spoon: Soup spoons go to the right of the knife, and tradition dictates the order in which cutlery is used.
Things you set a dinner table with.Napkin: Cloth napkins can be folded into elaborate shapes, and the art of napkin folding dates back to the 1600s.
Things you set a dinner table with.Wine glass: A formal setting places wine glasses at the top right, above the knives.
Things you set a dinner table with.Placemat: Placemats protect the table from heat and spills, and they became popular in Victorian times.
Things you set a dinner table with.Tablecloth: A tablecloth was once a sign of status, and formal ones should hang about 25 to 30 centimeters past the edge.
Things you set a dinner table with.Salt shaker: Salt was once so valuable it was used as currency, and its etymology gave us the word salary.
Things you set a dinner table with.Soup bowl: A soup bowl goes on top of the dinner plate or a charger, and a rimmed one keeps spills in.
Things you set a dinner table with.Napkin ring: Napkin rings began as a way for families to mark which cloth napkin was theirs between launderings.
Things you set a dinner table with.Pepper mill: Pepper was so valuable in medieval Europe that it was sometimes counted peppercorn by peppercorn as payment.
Things you set a dinner table with.Spatula: A spatula is a cooking and serving tool, so it stays in the kitchen rather than at a place setting.
Things you set a dinner table with.Whisk: A whisk is for mixing in the kitchen, and nobody lays one next to the cutlery.
Things you set a dinner table with.Colander: A colander drains food in the kitchen, and it never makes it to the dinner table.
Things you set a dinner table with.Rolling pin: A rolling pin is for pastry preparation, well before anyone sits down to eat.
Things you set a dinner table with.Oven mitt: Oven mitts are for taking hot dishes out, but they're set aside before the meal starts.
Things you set a dinner table with.Frying pan: A frying pan is where food is cooked, but it's typically served onto plates, not placed on the table.
Things you set a dinner table with.Tea towel: A tea towel is for drying dishes in the kitchen, and a napkin is its dining counterpart.
Things you set a dinner table with.Sponge: A sponge is for cleaning up after dinner, and it's not part of the table setting.
Things you set a dinner table with.Can opener: A can opener is used before cooking, and its invention came 45 years after canning itself, in 1855.
Things you set a dinner table with.Measuring cup: A measuring cup is for recipe prep, which is long done by the time the table is set.
Things you set a dinner table with.Toaster: A toaster is a breakfast appliance on the counter, and it's not part of a dinner setting.
Things you set a dinner table with.Dish rack: A dish rack is for drying washed dishes, so it's an after-dinner tool.

Things shown on a driver's license.Photo: License photos are checked by face-matching software in many places, which is why smiling is discouraged in some regions.
Things shown on a driver's license.Full name: Names must match your other ID, and misspelled names are one of the most common reasons for rejected applications.
Things shown on a driver's license.Date of birth: Bars and shops check it for age-restricted sales, and many US licenses switch to a vertical layout for under-21 holders.
Things shown on a driver's license.Address: Your address on the card has to be updated after a move, and many places fine drivers who fail to do so.
Things shown on a driver's license.License number: Some US states encode your name and birth date into the number, so it is more than random digits.
Things shown on a driver's license.Expiry date: Licenses expire from every few years to every decade, depending on the place, and renewal can include an eye test.
Things shown on a driver's license.Signature: Your signature on the card helps verify identity at a bank or on a rental form.
Things shown on a driver's license.Issue date: The issue date shows when the card was printed, and it can differ from when you first passed your test.
Things shown on a driver's license.License class: The class, or category, shows which vehicles you can drive, such as car, motorcycle or heavy truck.
Things shown on a driver's license.Shoe size: A trap: a license says who you are and what you may drive. Height and eye color appear on many, but nobody needs your shoe size.
Things shown on a driver's license.Favorite color: Eye and hair color appear on some licenses, but not a favorite color.
Things shown on a driver's license.Email address: Email addresses are not on the card, though some governments are starting to link digital licenses to phones.
Things shown on a driver's license.Salary: Income is private information the licensing office has no reason to collect.
Things shown on a driver's license.Pet's name: Pet names are common passwords, so it is just as well they stay off your license.
Things shown on a driver's license.Credit score: Credit scores come from credit bureaus, and a motor vehicle department never sees one.
Things shown on a driver's license.Star sign: Your birthday is on the license, so you could work out the zodiac sign, but it is not printed.
Things shown on a driver's license.Car color: Car color is part of vehicle registration, not the driver's license.
Things shown on a driver's license.Car model: The registration lists the car, and the license concerns the person.
Things shown on a driver's license.Job title: Occupation does not appear on a license, though old passports used to list it.
Things shown on a driver's license.Bank balance: A license has nothing to do with money, and a bank balance would be a serious privacy risk.
Things shown on a driver's license.Religion: Religion is private, and many countries bar IDs from listing it.
Things shown on a driver's license.Phone number: Phone numbers change too often, so they are normally kept in a database, not printed on the card.
Things shown on a driver's license.Hobbies: Hobbies are not recorded, though some places let you add an organ donor mark to the card.
Things shown on a driver's license.Marital status: Marital status is not printed, because it would date the card as soon as someone married.

Things for dealing with snow and ice.Snow shovel: Snow shovels with a curved blade lift more per scoop, but snow is heavier than it looks: a shovelful can weigh over 10 pounds.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Snowblower: Snowblowers were invented in Canada in the 1800s for railways, and home versions followed in the 1950s.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Ice scraper: Pressing a scraper at an angle across the glass lets its edge lift the ice sheet instead of just skating over it.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Rock salt: Rock salt lowers water's freezing point, but below about minus 10 C it stops working well on roads.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Grit: Grit is sand or fine gravel spread on ice. It doesn't melt anything, it just gives tires and shoes something to bite.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Snowplow: Snowplows go back to horse-drawn wedges in the 1800s, and today's trucks often carry a brine tank too.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Snow brush: A snow brush has long soft bristles that sweep snow off a car without scratching the paint.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Ice chipper: An ice chipper is a sharp-edged tool for breaking up stubborn ice from steps and driveways.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Roof rake: A roof rake has a long pole to pull snow off from the ground, preventing heavy loads and ice dams.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Ice melt: Ice melt is often calcium chloride or magnesium chloride, which release heat as they dissolve and work at lower temperatures than salt.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Lawnmower: A lawnmower cuts grass in summer. It would just clog and jam in snow.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Garden hose: A garden hose waters plants in warm weather and must be drained in winter, or the water inside can freeze and split it.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Sprinkler: Sprinklers are for dry spells. Their pipes are usually blown out before freezing temperatures arrive.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Leaf rake: Leaf rakes have flexible tines for gathering leaves. A snow's weight would bend them to uselessness.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Hedge trimmer: Hedge trimmers shape shrubs in the growing season and have no use for snow clearing.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Watering can: A watering can helps houseplants and flower beds. Not much use for ice.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Pruning shears: Pruning shears are best used in late winter, but only on plants, not on the snowy driveway.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Trowel: A trowel digs holes for planting. Frozen soil is hard to dig with one, so it's mostly a spring tool.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Beach umbrella: A beach umbrella blocks the sun. In snow, you'd want a hat instead.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Pool skimmer: A pool skimmer scoops leaves and bugs from a swimming pool, and it's of no help clearing a driveway.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Desk fan: A desk fan moves air to cool a room. It's the opposite of what a snowy day calls for.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Paddling pool: A paddling pool is a summer toy for toddlers. Snow turns it into a bucket for ice.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Sunscreen: Sunscreen is a trap: snow reflects up to about 80 percent of UV, so skiers get burned, but it won't clear any snow.
Things for dealing with snow and ice.Weed whacker: A weed whacker uses spinning nylon line, which trims grass. It can't push snow.

Over-the-counter painkillers.Ibuprofen: Ibuprofen is an NSAID that reduces inflammation as well as pain, and is easier on the stomach when taken with food.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Aspirin: Aspirin descends from willow bark remedies, and Bayer brought it to market in 1899.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Acetaminophen: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever but barely touches inflammation, and an overdose can seriously damage the liver.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Naproxen: Naproxen lasts longer than ibuprofen, so doses are spaced about 8 to 12 hours apart.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Paracetamol: Paracetamol is the name used outside the US and Canada for acetaminophen; it is the same drug.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Advil: Advil is a brand of ibuprofen, launched in the US in 1984.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Tylenol: Tylenol is the best-known acetaminophen brand, its name trimmed from the drug's long chemical name.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Aleve: Aleve is naproxen sodium, a longer-lasting NSAID sold over the counter since 1994.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Motrin: Motrin is another ibuprofen brand, so taking it with Advil would double the same drug.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Penicillin: Penicillin is an antibiotic that needs a prescription, and it fights bacteria, not pain.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Amoxicillin: Amoxicillin is a prescription antibiotic, not a painkiller.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Insulin: Insulin treats diabetes, and the hormone was first given to a patient in 1922.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Benadryl: Benadryl is an antihistamine for allergies, and its drowsiness is why it appears in sleep aids.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Zyrtec: Zyrtec is an allergy antihistamine (cetirizine), not a painkiller.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Claritin: Claritin (loratadine) treats allergies and is less drowsy than older antihistamines.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Tums: Tums neutralize stomach acid with calcium carbonate, which is basically chalk.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Pepto-Bismol: Pepto-Bismol settles upset stomachs, and its pink bismuth subsalicylate is a relative of aspirin.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Melatonin: Melatonin is a sleep hormone your brain makes in darkness, not a pain reliever.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Imodium: Imodium (loperamide) slows the gut to stop diarrhea, not to ease pain.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Lactaid: Lactaid supplies lactase enzyme to digest milk sugar, and does nothing for pain.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Dramamine: Dramamine treats motion sickness, and the drowsiness is a side effect of its antihistamine.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Eye drops: Eye drops moisten or treat eyes, not general pain.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Antacid: An antacid neutralizes stomach acid for heartburn, which is different from easing pain.
Over-the-counter painkillers.Vitamin C: Vitamin C does not relieve pain, though the body needs it to make collagen.

Things in an ambulance.Stretcher: Ambulance stretchers have folding legs that collapse automatically as they roll into the vehicle, which saves lifting.
Things in an ambulance.Defibrillator: A defibrillator shocks the heart to reset its rhythm, and modern AEDs talk users through every step.
Things in an ambulance.Oxygen tank: Medical oxygen is nearly pure, compared with about 21 percent in the air we breathe, so patients get a big boost.
Things in an ambulance.Siren: Sirens use patterns like wail and yelp to help drivers notice them from different distances.
Things in an ambulance.Splints: Splints immobilize broken limbs to prevent further damage while the patient is being moved.
Things in an ambulance.Neck brace: A neck brace, properly a cervical collar, is placed after crashes to protect the spine from movement.
Things in an ambulance.Bandages: Ambulances carry tourniquets and pressure dressings, since severe bleeding can be fatal in minutes.
Things in an ambulance.Blood pressure cuff: The blood pressure cuff descends from the sphygmomanometer, first invented in 1881 by Samuel von Basch.
Things in an ambulance.Flashing lights: Some fleets use fluorescent lime-yellow paint, since people see it better than red, alongside the flashing lights.
Things in an ambulance.Radio: Radios let crews alert the hospital in advance, so staff are ready when the patient arrives.
Things in an ambulance.Jukebox: A trap: a jukebox belongs in a diner, not an ambulance, where every item has a medical job.
Things in an ambulance.Bunk bed: A trap: ambulances carry one stretcher, not bunks; it is fire stations that have bunk rooms.
Things in an ambulance.Popcorn machine: A trap: a popcorn machine belongs in a cinema, not in an ambulance, which carries only medical gear.
Things in an ambulance.Treadmill: A trap: treadmills were invented in 1818 as a prison punishment, and they are not carried in an ambulance.
Things in an ambulance.Fish tank: A trap: a fish tank has no place in an ambulance, where nothing is allowed to slosh around.
Things in an ambulance.Pizza oven: A trap: a pizza oven would be pointless in an ambulance, which carries only medical gear.
Things in an ambulance.Washing machine: A trap: washing machines stay in laundry rooms; ambulances are cleaned and restocked after each call.
Things in an ambulance.Bookshelf: A trap: a bookshelf has no place in an ambulance, where every item is secured and medical.
Things in an ambulance.Hot tub: A trap: a hot tub belongs to spas, not emergency vehicles, which carry only gear that treats patients.
Things in an ambulance.Dartboard: A trap: a dartboard in an ambulance would be a hazard, not a medical tool.
Things in an ambulance.Ping-pong table: A trap: table tennis began as a Victorian parlor game and has no place in an ambulance.
Things in an ambulance.Disco ball: A trap: a disco ball would be flashy, but ambulances rely on practical flashing lights.
Things in an ambulance.Piano: A trap: a piano is too large and heavy for any ambulance, which carries only medical gear.
Things in an ambulance.Bathtub: A trap: a bathtub is too bulky for an ambulance, which carries a stretcher instead.

Things most cats hate.Bath: Cats hate baths since their fur is not waterproof and becomes heavy, though they groom themselves and rarely need one.
Things most cats hate.Vacuum cleaner: A vacuum is loud and intimidating, and a cat's hearing reaches far higher pitches than ours, so the noise is worse for it.
Things most cats hate.Car ride: Many cats get anxious and carsick in cars, since they are creatures of territory and a moving car takes them away from it.
Things most cats hate.Vet visit: Cats hide illness by instinct, so a vet visit's strange smells and noise are stressful, and carriers help.
Things most cats hate.Spray bottle: A spray bottle of water is a common but disliked training tool, and trainers now suggest rewards work better.
Things most cats hate.Thunder: Cats can hear sounds up to about 64 kilohertz, so thunder and storms are far noisier for them.
Things most cats hate.Fireworks: Fireworks are loud and unpredictable, and cats hear far higher pitches than we do, so many hide for hours afterward.
Things most cats hate.Hair dryer: The hiss and hot air of a hair dryer is unpleasant for a cat, which can hear the high-pitched whine of its motor.
Things most cats hate.Closed door: Cats hate closed doors, since they like to patrol their territory and may meow or scratch to open them.
Things most cats hate.Cucumber surprise: Viral videos show cats leaping from cucumbers placed behind them, probably because it looks like a snake.
Things most cats hate.Catnip: Catnip affects about two thirds of cats through a chemical called nepetalactone, and it is harmless to them.
Things most cats hate.Laser pointer: A laser pointer triggers a cat's hunting instinct, but since the cat never catches it, vets suggest ending with a toy to catch.
Things most cats hate.Cardboard box: Cats love boxes since a snug space makes them feel safe, and studies found boxes reduce stress in shelter cats.
Things most cats hate.Sunbeam: Cats seek out sunbeams because they prefer warmer temperatures than people, about 30 to 38 degrees Celsius.
Things most cats hate.Tuna: Cats love the smell of tuna, though a diet of only tuna lacks nutrients and can cause health problems.
Things most cats hate.Ball of yarn: Cats chase yarn by hunting instinct, but swallowing string can be dangerous for them, so it is a plaything to supervise.
Things most cats hate.Chin scratches: Cats have scent glands around their cheeks and chin, so they love scratches there as it spreads their scent.
Things most cats hate.Warm laptop: A warm laptop is irresistible to cats, who seek heat, and sit on keyboards where your attention is.
Things most cats hate.Feather toy: A feather toy imitates a bird, and the cat's hunting instincts make it one of the most reliable cat toys.
Things most cats hate.Cozy blanket: Cats knead blankets, a habit that begins in kittenhood, when they knead their mother to get the milk flowing.
Things most cats hate.Treats: Treats work well for cats, but they should be no more than about a tenth of a cat's daily calories.
Things most cats hate.Fresh salmon: Fresh salmon tastes great to cats, though raw fish can carry parasites and certain enzymes can cause trouble.
Things most cats hate.Windowsill: Cats love windowsills as an outlook post, and watching birds there is a favorite pastime, sometimes called cat TV.
Things most cats hate.Scratching post: Cats scratch to shed old claw sheaths and to mark territory with scent glands in their paws, so a post saves the sofa.

Jobs at a circus.Ringmaster: The ringmaster is the master of ceremonies, usually in a red coat and top hat, who introduces each act and keeps the show moving.
Jobs at a circus.Clown: Clowns have a long tradition, and Joseph Grimaldi in early 1800s London shaped the modern clown, with a white face and bold makeup.
Jobs at a circus.Acrobat: Acrobats rely on strength, balance and trust, and the best are trained for years, often from childhood, in families of circus performers.
Jobs at a circus.Juggler: Jugglers have been depicted in Egyptian tomb paintings thousands of years old, so it's one of the oldest performing arts.
Jobs at a circus.Trapeze artist: A trapeze artist swings through the air, and the first flying trapeze act was performed by Jules Léotard in the 1850s, whose name lives on in the leotard.
Jobs at a circus.Tightrope walker: A tightrope walker crosses a thin cable with only balance, and Philippe Petit famously walked between the Twin Towers in 1974.
Jobs at a circus.Lion tamer: The lion tamer used a chair and a whip in a famous act, but the act is rare now, since many places have banned animal acts.
Jobs at a circus.Fire-eater: The fire-eater puts burning torches in their mouth, and the trick is mostly in controlling breath and avoiding inhaling the flame.
Jobs at a circus.Contortionist: A contortionist bends their body into impossible shapes, and training starts very young, often with years of stretching.
Jobs at a circus.Strongman: A strongman lifts huge weights, and in the 1800s, strongmen were circus headliners, long before gyms and bodybuilding.
Jobs at a circus.Stilt walker: A stilt walker moves around on tall poles, and the skill goes back centuries, even to shepherds who used stilts in marshy land.
Jobs at a circus.Sommelier: A sommelier advises on wine in restaurants, so they're all wrong for the big top, unless the circus has a very fancy bar.
Jobs at a circus.Bailiff: A bailiff enforces court orders, so they're about the least circus-like job here, even if a circus can go bust.
Jobs at a circus.Golf caddie: Golf caddies carry bags for golfers on courses, so they're not part of any act.
Jobs at a circus.Astronaut: Astronauts fly in space. A circus trapeze act feels like zero gravity, but it's not the same job at all.
Jobs at a circus.Butler: Butlers run a household and wait on a family, so it's a job for a manor house, not for a circus tent.
Jobs at a circus.Lifeguard: Lifeguards watch over swimmers, so they don't belong to the circus, though a water show may have one.
Jobs at a circus.Surgeon: Surgeons operate on patients. A circus acts like a risk but any medical care there is from a doctor on call.
Jobs at a circus.Bricklayer: Bricklayers build walls. A circus is built of tents and poles, so it doesn't need one.
Jobs at a circus.Plumber: Plumbers fix pipes. A traveling circus may have a handyman, but not a dedicated plumber.
Jobs at a circus.Diplomat: Diplomats represent countries abroad. A circus may tour internationally, but its performers aren't official envoys.
Jobs at a circus.Senator: Senators make laws. Not circus work, though political life is sometimes called a circus.
Jobs at a circus.Notary: Notaries certify documents, and they sit in offices, not in tents, however busy the circus paperwork.
Jobs at a circus.Dentist: Dentists treat teeth, so they're not in the circus, though some old shows did have a travelling tooth-puller.

Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Hobbit: A small, stout, hairy-footed folk, who first appeared in Tolkien's The Hobbit; the word is Tolkien's invention, perhaps from 'hole-builder'.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Ent: Tree-like shepherds of the forest who are slow to anger, their name coming from the Old English for 'giant'; Treebeard is the best-known.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Orc: Tolkien's brutish servants of the Dark Lord, originally bred by corrupting Elves; the word orc comes from Old English orcneas.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Balrog: A fire-demon of Morgoth's, a Maia, he killed Gandalf the Grey in Moria; Gandalf's reply was 'You shall not pass!'
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Uruk-hai: Stronger, larger orcs bred by Saruman at Isengard, they were able to walk in sunlight, unlike common orcs.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Warg: Fierce wolf-like beasts ridden by orcs that attack the Fellowship; the name comes from Old Norse 'vargr', meaning wolf or outlaw.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Nazgûl: The Ringwraiths, nine kings of Men turned into ghosts by the rings, are Sauron's deadliest servants, hunting Frodo on horseback.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Oliphaunt: Giant war-elephants of Harad; the name comes from Sam's rhyme about the beast, and the Gondorian word is Mûmak.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Huorn: Trees that grew sentient and walked, the Huorns are related to Ents, and helped win at Helm's Deep.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Barrow-wight: Evil spirits in barrow-mounds, they trapped Frodo and his friends until Tom Bombadil's rescue, in the Old Forest.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Fell beast: A flying, dragon-like steed of the Nazgûl, which carries the Witch-king; Éowyn and Merry brought him down.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Dementor: Harry Potter's soul-sucking guards of Azkaban are from another author's world, not Tolkien's.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Hippogriff: Half-eagle, half-horse creatures from Harry Potter, not Middle-earth, who bow to be approached.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Thestral: Harry Potter's skeletal, winged horses, visible only to those who have seen death, aren't Tolkien's.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Faun: Half-goat creatures from Narnia, like Mr. Tumnus, not Middle-earth.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Marsh-wiggle: A frog-like Narnian from C. S. Lewis, not Tolkien, though the two authors were close friends.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Dalek: The mechanical alien enemy from Doctor Who, who shouts 'Exterminate!', isn't from Middle-earth.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Wookiee: Chewbacca's furry species, from Star Wars, isn't Tolkien's.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Ewok: Small furry creatures from Star Wars, who helped beat the Empire, aren't Tolkien's.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Gremlin: Little mischievous creatures from airplane folklore, popularized by Roald Dahl, aren't Tolkien's.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Smurf: Tiny blue creatures from the comic by Peyo, not Middle-earth.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Oompa-Loompa: The factory workers in Roald Dahl's Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, not from Tolkien.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Jabberwock: A monster from Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem Jabberwocky, not Tolkien's.
Creatures of Tolkien's Middle-earth.Niffler: A shiny-loving, burrowing creature from Fantastic Beasts, J. K. Rowling's world, not Tolkien's.

Places in Middle-earth.The Shire: The Shire was modeled on the Worcestershire countryside of Tolkien's childhood, near Sarehole mill.
Places in Middle-earth.Mordor: Mordor means Black Land in Sindarin, and Sauron's realm is walled by mountains and guarded by the Black Gate.
Places in Middle-earth.Rivendell: Rivendell, or Imladris, is Elrond's hidden valley refuge, where the Fellowship was formed.
Places in Middle-earth.Gondor: Gondor, whose name means Stone-land, is the greatest kingdom of Men and is ruled by stewards until Aragorn returns.
Places in Middle-earth.Rohan: Rohan's horse-lords have names and culture based on Old English, which Tolkien taught at Oxford.
Places in Middle-earth.Moria: Moria, once the dwarf city Khazad-dûm, was dug so deep that miners awakened the Balrog; Balin tried to retake it.
Places in Middle-earth.Isengard: Isengard holds the tower of Orthanc, where Saruman is trapped after the Ents flood the fortress by breaking a dam.
Places in Middle-earth.Lothlórien: Lothlórien is a forest of golden mallorn trees ruled by Galadriel and Celeborn, where elves live in tree platforms.
Places in Middle-earth.Mount Doom: Mount Doom, or Orodruin, is a volcano in Mordor where the One Ring was forged and where it has to be destroyed.
Places in Middle-earth.Minas Tirith: Minas Tirith, Gondor's capital, rises in seven levels cut into a mountain, and its name means Tower of the Guard.
Places in Middle-earth.Helm's Deep: Helm's Deep is a fortress in Rohan, whose Hornburg and the Deeping Wall are the site of a famous night siege.
Places in Middle-earth.Bree: Bree is a town where Men and hobbits live together and where the Prancing Pony inn is found.
Places in Middle-earth.Fangorn: Fangorn is Treebeard's ancient forest; its name is the Sindarin for beard of the tree, matching its oldest Ent.
Places in Middle-earth.Mirkwood: Mirkwood is a dark forest that Bilbo's company crosses; its giant spiders catch the dwarves.
Places in Middle-earth.Narnia: Narnia is C. S. Lewis's world, and Lewis, a friend of Tolkien, belonged to the same Oxford group, the Inklings.
Places in Middle-earth.Hogwarts: Hogwarts is J. K. Rowling's school of witchcraft and wizardry, set in Scotland, and has nothing to do with Tolkien's world.
Places in Middle-earth.Neverland: Neverland is J. M. Barrie's island for Peter Pan and the Lost Boys, not part of Tolkien's map.
Places in Middle-earth.Oz: Oz is L. Frank Baum's magical land, first visited in 1900; Baum later wrote thirteen sequels after the first book's success.
Places in Middle-earth.Wonderland: Wonderland is Lewis Carroll's world, which Alice reaches by falling down a rabbit hole; he first told it to a real girl on a boat trip.
Places in Middle-earth.Hogsmeade: Hogsmeade is the only all-wizard village in Britain, near Hogwarts, so it's not Middle-earth.
Places in Middle-earth.Camelot: Camelot is King Arthur's court; the name first appears in a 12th-century romance by Chrétien de Troyes.
Places in Middle-earth.Westeros: Westeros is George R. R. Martin's continent in A Song of Ice and Fire, with a wall of ice along its northern border.
Places in Middle-earth.Lilliput: Lilliput is Jonathan Swift's island of people about six inches tall in Gulliver's Travels.
Places in Middle-earth.Atlantis: Atlantis is a legendary sunken island that Plato described in his dialogues, not a Tolkien place.

Famous poems.The Raven: The Raven is Poe's 1845 poem about a bird that repeats Nevermore to a grieving man, and it made him famous.
Famous poems.Ozymandias: Ozymandias is Shelley's sonnet about a ruined statue's boast, and the king is thought to be Ramesses II.
Famous poems.The Road Not Taken: The Road Not Taken is widely misread as a celebration of individuality, though Frost meant it as a tease of a friend.
Famous poems.Jabberwocky: Jabberwocky is Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem that gave English words like chortle and galumph.
Famous poems.Kubla Khan: Kubla Khan is Coleridge's poem that, he said, was interrupted when a visitor from Porlock arrived.
Famous poems.The Waste Land: The Waste Land is T. S. Eliot's 1922 modernist poem, which Ezra Pound heavily edited.
Famous poems.Howl: Howl is Allen Ginsberg's 1956 poem, which prompted an obscenity trial in 1957 that Ginsberg won.
Famous poems.Invictus: Invictus is William Ernest Henley's poem that Nelson Mandela reportedly recited in prison, ending I am the captain of my soul.
Famous poems.Annabel Lee: Annabel Lee is one of Poe's last poems, a tribute to a lost love, published after his death.
Famous poems.The Tyger: The Tyger is William Blake's poem that asks what immortal hand or eye could frame such a fearsome creature.
Famous poems.Ode to a Nightingale: Ode to a Nightingale is Keats's 1819 poem about escaping into birdsong, written in a single morning.
Famous poems.Daffodils: Daffodils, or I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud, was inspired by a walk recorded in Dorothy Wordsworth's journal.
Famous poems.Sonnet 18: Sonnet 18 is Shakespeare's Shall I compare thee to a summer's day, promising immortality through verse.
Famous poems.Moby-Dick: Moby-Dick is Melville's 1851 novel, not a poem, even though it's full of poetic prose.
Famous poems.Hamlet: Hamlet is Shakespeare's tragedy, a play and not a poem, though written in verse.
Famous poems.Middlemarch: Middlemarch is George Eliot's long novel of provincial life, a prose work, not a poem.
Famous poems.Dracula: Dracula is Bram Stoker's 1897 novel, told through letters and diary entries, not a poem.
Famous poems.Persuasion: Persuasion is Jane Austen's last completed novel, published after her death, and it's prose.
Famous poems.Rebecca: Rebecca is Daphne du Maurier's 1938 novel, and it opens with the line about dreaming of Manderley.
Famous poems.Emma: Emma is Jane Austen's novel about a young matchmaker, so it's a prose tale, not a poem.
Famous poems.Lolita: Lolita is Vladimir Nabokov's controversial 1955 novel, so it's prose, not poetry.
Famous poems.Candide: Candide is Voltaire's 1759 satirical novella, in prose, not a poem.
Famous poems.Walden: Walden is Thoreau's prose account of two years by a Massachusetts pond, not a poem.
Famous poems.Beloved: Beloved is Toni Morrison's Pulitzer-winning novel about slavery's legacy, so it's prose, not poetry.

British artists.J. M. W. Turner: The Turner Prize is named after him, and he bequeathed thousands of his works to the British nation.
British artists.John Constable: The Hay Wain (1821) won a gold medal at the Paris Salon, where it was admired more than at home.
British artists.David Hockney: Famous for LA swimming pools, and in his seventies he started drawing on an iPad, a new tool for an English painter.
British artists.Banksy: This anonymous street artist's Girl with Balloon shredded itself right after selling at Sotheby's in 2018.
British artists.Damien Hirst: He's known for a shark in formaldehyde called The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living.
British artists.Tracey Emin: Her My Bed, an unmade bed strewn with debris, was shortlisted for the 1999 Turner Prize and caused uproar.
British artists.Thomas Gainsborough: He preferred landscapes, but he earned his living from portraits like The Blue Boy, now in California's Huntington.
British artists.William Hogarth: His satirical series like A Rake's Progress led to the first copyright law, the Hogarth Act of 1735.
British artists.William Blake: Poet and engraver who claimed to see angels in a tree on Peckham Rye, and who illustrated his own books.
British artists.Henry Moore: His reclining figure sculptures sit in public spaces around the world, and he was born in Yorkshire to a miner.
British artists.L. S. Lowry: His "matchstick men" scenes depict industrial northern England, and he declined several honours.
British artists.Joshua Reynolds: First president of the Royal Academy in 1768, and a famous lecturer on painting who set the tone of British art.
British artists.George Stubbs: He spent eighteen months dissecting horses to master their anatomy, and published a book of the drawings.
British artists.Edward Hopper: An American realist, famous for Nighthawks, so he doesn't belong among British artists, despite his fame in Britain.
British artists.Andy Warhol: An American Pop artist, born in Pittsburgh, so he is not part of the British group, however famous in London.
British artists.James Whistler: American-born, though he lived in London, so he's not British, even if his Mother is famous in Britain.
British artists.Claude Monet: The French Impressionist painted London's fog and the Thames in the early 1900s, but he's French.
British artists.Canaletto: The Venetian view painter spent about nine years in England, but he's Italian, so he doesn't qualify.
British artists.Hans Holbein: German painter at Henry VIII's court, so he lived in England but wasn't British, despite painting the Tudors.
British artists.Anthony van Dyck: Flemish painter who became court painter to Charles I and was knighted, but is not British.
British artists.Jackson Pollock: An American, famous for dripping paint onto canvases, so he does not count as a British artist at all.
British artists.Georgia O'Keeffe: An American, famed for her huge flowers and New Mexico landscapes, so she is not a British artist.
British artists.Salvador Dalí: A Spanish Surrealist famous for melting clocks, and not from Britain at all, though he exhibited in London.
British artists.Edvard Munch: A Norwegian, who painted The Scream and other haunted scenes, so he isn't a British artist.

Famous photographers.Ansel Adams: His Yosemite landscapes, and the Zone System he devised with Fred Archer, set a standard for black-and-white tonal control.
Famous photographers.Annie Leibovitz: She photographed John Lennon and Yoko Ono for Rolling Stone on December 8, 1980, only hours before Lennon was shot.
Famous photographers.Dorothea Lange: Her 1936 "Migrant Mother" became the defining image of the Great Depression.
Famous photographers.Cartier-Bresson: He called the peak instant of a scene "the decisive moment" and co-founded the Magnum agency.
Famous photographers.Robert Capa: "Capa" began as an invented persona he and partner Gerda Taro made up; he was killed by a land mine in Indochina in 1954.
Famous photographers.Diane Arbus: She photographed people on society's margins, and in 1972 became the first American photographer shown at the Venice Biennale.
Famous photographers.Richard Avedon: His stark white-background portraits and fashion work ran in Harper's Bazaar and Vogue; his book In the American West drew praise and controversy.
Famous photographers.Man Ray: The American in Paris made "rayographs", camera-less images created by placing objects directly on photographic paper.
Famous photographers.Alfred Stieglitz: He ran the New York gallery 291, championed photography as art, and was married to painter Georgia O'Keeffe.
Famous photographers.Cindy Sherman: She is her own model in Untitled Film Stills, playing invented characters, like movie heroines.
Famous photographers.Vivian Maier: A Chicago nanny whose thousands of unseen negatives were discovered at auction around 2007, after which she became famous.
Famous photographers.Steve McCurry: His 1985 portrait of a green-eyed Afghan refugee girl is among National Geographic's best-known covers.
Famous photographers.Irving Penn: For Vogue he posed sitters in a tight angled corner of two flats, a trademark of his portraits from 1948.
Famous photographers.Edward Hopper: A painter of lonely scenes like Nighthawks (1942); he didn't make photographs.
Famous photographers.Georgia O'Keeffe: She painted giant flowers and desert bones; she's often confused with her husband Stieglitz, the photographer who championed her.
Famous photographers.Norman Rockwell: Rockwell was an illustrator for the Saturday Evening Post, who did use photographs as references for his paintings.
Famous photographers.Frida Kahlo: Kahlo was a Mexican painter famous for her self-portraits, not a photographer, though her father was one.
Famous photographers.Claude Monet: Monet painted water lilies and haystacks to catch changing light; he was an Impressionist painter.
Famous photographers.Salvador Dalí: Dalí's melting clocks made him a surrealist painter, though he also posed for many photographers.
Famous photographers.Jackson Pollock: Pollock dripped paint onto canvases laid on the floor, an action painter.
Famous photographers.Banksy: Banksy is an anonymous street artist known for stencils, not a photographer.
Famous photographers.Bob Ross: Bob Ross painted a landscape in under half an hour on TV's The Joy of Painting.
Famous photographers.Mark Rothko: Rothko painted floating blocks of color; the Rothko Chapel in Houston is lined with them.
Famous photographers.Grant Wood: Wood painted American Gothic (1930), a painting; his models were his dentist and his sister.

Shades of blue.Navy: The name comes from the dark blue uniforms of the British Royal Navy, adopted in 1748.
Shades of blue.Azure: The word comes from the Persian 'lazhward', the source of lapis lazuli, and it is the blue of a clear sky.
Shades of blue.Cobalt: Cobalt blue pigment, made from cobalt aluminate, has colored ceramics and glass since ancient times.
Shades of blue.Sky blue: The sky is blue because air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths more strongly than red ones.
Shades of blue.Royal blue: A vivid, deep blue whose name dates to the 1700s, and it's shown up in royal courts and uniforms ever since.
Shades of blue.Cerulean: Cerulean comes from the Latin 'caeruleus' for sky, and in The Devil Wears Prada it is the subject of a famous monologue.
Shades of blue.Ultramarine: This pigment was once ground from lapis lazuli brought across the sea from Afghanistan, and it cost more than gold.
Shades of blue.Baby blue: A pale, soft blue named for the color long used in baby clothes; it's one of the lighter shades in the range.
Shades of blue.Powder blue: The name came from smalt, a ground blue glass, which was used to color laundry and make powder.
Shades of blue.Prussian blue: Prussian blue was the first modern synthetic pigment, discovered by accident in Berlin around 1706, and Hokusai used it in his Great Wave.
Shades of blue.Midnight blue: A very dark blue, close to black, that is named after the night sky.
Shades of blue.Sapphire: Sapphire is blue from traces of iron and titanium in corundum, and the color is as old as the gemstone.
Shades of blue.Crimson: Crimson is a deep red, originally from the dye of kermes insects.
Shades of blue.Scarlet: Scarlet is a bright red, and once meant a fine cloth rather than a color.
Shades of blue.Lavender: Lavender is a pale purple, named after the flower.
Shades of blue.Emerald: Emerald is green, though blue-green shades exist.
Shades of blue.Chartreuse: Chartreuse is a yellow-green named after the French liqueur, which was named after a monastery.
Shades of blue.Magenta: Magenta is a purplish red, named after the 1859 battle of Magenta in Italy, and dye was invented the same year.
Shades of blue.Ochre: Ochre is a yellow-brown earth pigment, used since prehistory, including in cave paintings.
Shades of blue.Maroon: Maroon is a dark brownish red, and the word comes from the French for chestnut.
Shades of blue.Mauve: Mauve was the first synthetic dye, made by a teenage William Perkin in 1856 while trying to make a malaria drug.
Shades of blue.Olive: Olive is a dull yellowish green, and it's named after the fruit.
Shades of blue.Amber: Amber is a golden orange-yellow, named after fossilized tree resin.
Shades of blue.Vermilion: Vermilion is a bright red-orange, traditionally made from the mineral cinnabar.

Animals with horns.Rhino: A rhino's horn is made of keratin, the same material as hair and nails, and it keeps growing throughout its life.
Animals with horns.Ram: A ram's horns grow in spirals and are never shed, and males ram heads at speeds that would knock out a person.
Animals with horns.Bull: A bull's horns are permanent and made of bone covered in keratin, unlike antlers that fall off yearly.
Animals with horns.Goat: Both male and female goats typically have horns, and their rectangular pupils give them a wide field of view.
Animals with horns.Unicorn: A trap: no real animal has a single spiral horn, though medieval 'unicorn horns' were actually narwhal tusks.
Animals with horns.Triceratops: Triceratops means 'three-horned face', and its huge frill and horns may have been used to fight rivals or deter predators.
Animals with horns.Antelope: True antelope horns are permanent, unbranched and never shed, and the spiral-horned kudu's can reach over a meter long.
Animals with horns.Bison: Both male and female bison have horns, and a bull can weigh nearly a ton while running at about 35 miles per hour.
Animals with horns.Yak: Wild and domestic yaks have curved horns and thrive above 4,000 meters, where their huge lungs handle thin air.
Animals with horns.Ibex: Ibex males carry long, ridged curved horns that can be over a meter long and let them clamber on sheer cliffs.
Animals with horns.Water buffalo: Water buffalo have wide, sweeping horns that can span over two meters, and they love to wallow in mud.
Animals with horns.Narwhal: A trap: the narwhal's 'horn' is actually a long spiral tooth, an overgrown canine that can reach about 3 meters.
Animals with horns.Moose: A moose grows antlers, not horns, shedding them every winter and regrowing a new, larger pair each year.
Animals with horns.Deer: Deer have antlers of solid bone that are shed yearly, unlike permanent keratin-sheathed horns.
Animals with horns.Elk: Elk antlers can grow an inch a day in spring, which makes them one of the fastest-growing animal tissues known.
Animals with horns.Walrus: A walrus has two long tusks, which are really elongated canine teeth that it uses to haul itself onto ice.
Animals with horns.Elephant: An elephant's tusks are overgrown incisors, not horns, and they continue to grow throughout its life.
Animals with horns.Horse: Horses have no horns or antlers at all, which is partly why the unicorn myth added one.
Animals with horns.Wild boar: Wild boars have tusks, which are actually canine teeth, instead of horns.
Animals with horns.Kangaroo: Kangaroos have no horns, but males have powerful legs and can box with their forelimbs and kick hard.
Animals with horns.Lion: Lions have no horns, but a male's mane may signal strength to rivals and females.
Animals with horns.Zebra: Zebras are hornless, and each one's stripe pattern is unique, as a fingerprint is.
Animals with horns.Donkey: Donkeys have long ears but no horns, and their hearing helps them detect other donkeys miles away in deserts.
Animals with horns.Caribou: Caribou are the only deer species in which females also grow antlers, which are bone and shed, not horns.

Kinds of bicycle.BMX: BMX stands for bicycle motocross, and it became an Olympic sport in 2008.
Kinds of bicycle.Mountain bike: Mountain biking took off in 1970s Marin County, California, where riders raced old balloon-tire cruisers down a hill nicknamed Repack.
Kinds of bicycle.Tandem: Tandem comes from the Latin for 'at length', and it first described horses harnessed one behind another.
Kinds of bicycle.Penny-farthing: The penny-farthing is named for a large penny and a small farthing coin, and riders risked falling head-first when the big wheel stopped.
Kinds of bicycle.Road bike: Under UCI racing rules, a road bike must weigh at least 6.8 kilograms, so makers add weights to lighter bikes.
Kinds of bicycle.Recumbent: The UCI banned recumbent bikes from racing in 1934 after one rider beat records on one.
Kinds of bicycle.Fixie: Fixies have a single gear fixed to the wheel, so the pedals keep turning as the bike rolls, and you can't coast.
Kinds of bicycle.Cruiser: Cruisers have wide, balloon tires and a relaxed seat, a style that began in the 1930s American Schwinn Excelsior.
Kinds of bicycle.Folding bike: Folding bikes like the Brompton, built by hand in London, can fold into a package in about 20 seconds.
Kinds of bicycle.E-bike: E-bikes add a pedal-assist motor, and in some European countries they now outsell electric cars.
Kinds of bicycle.Fat bike: Fat bikes use huge 4-inch tires to float over snow and sand, and are popular on winter trails.
Kinds of bicycle.Moped: A moped has pedals in name only, but its motor does the work, so it is not a bicycle.
Kinds of bicycle.Scooter: A scooter is pushed with a foot or driven by a small motor, and it has no pedals or chain.
Kinds of bicycle.Unicycle: A unicycle has one wheel, and the 'bi' in bicycle means two, so it falls short.
Kinds of bicycle.Tricycle: A tricycle has three wheels, so it fails the bi test, but adults ride them too.
Kinds of bicycle.Segway: A Segway is a self-balancing electric scooter, and it has two wheels but no pedals.
Kinds of bicycle.Skateboard: A skateboard has four small wheels and no pedals, so it isn't a bicycle.
Kinds of bicycle.Hoverboard: A hoverboard has two motorized wheels and no handlebars, and it isn't a bicycle.
Kinds of bicycle.Quad bike: A quad bike has four wheels and an engine, and it isn't a bicycle.
Kinds of bicycle.Pogo stick: A pogo stick bounces on a spring, and it has no wheels at all.
Kinds of bicycle.Motorcycle: A motorcycle has an engine, and the engine makes it a different class of vehicle.
Kinds of bicycle.Jet ski: A jet ski rides on water, and it isn't a bicycle.
Kinds of bicycle.Go-kart: A go-kart is a small racing car, not a bicycle.
Kinds of bicycle.Rollerblades: Rollerblades are in-line skates, and they aren't a kind of bicycle.

Ghosts in fiction.Casper: The Friendly Ghost debuted in a 1940s cartoon from Famous Studios. His 1995 movie was one of the first to use heavy CGI for a lead character.
Ghosts in fiction.Slimer: Ghostbusters' green blob ghost, reportedly inspired by John Belushi, who had starred in comedies with Dan Aykroyd.
Ghosts in fiction.Nearly Headless Nick: The Gryffindor ghost whose beheading was botched. His neck was hacked about 45 times, leaving him hanging by a sliver of skin.
Ghosts in fiction.Moaning Myrtle: The ghost who haunts a girls' bathroom at Hogwarts. She died there, killed by the basilisk.
Ghosts in fiction.Jacob Marley: Scrooge's dead partner in A Christmas Carol (1843) wears the chains he forged in life, link by link.
Ghosts in fiction.Beetlejuice: Tim Burton's 1988 ghost, a self-styled bio-exorcist, who is on screen for well under 20 minutes.
Ghosts in fiction.Canterville Ghost: Oscar Wilde's 1887 comic tale in which a ghost is outwitted by a practical American family.
Ghosts in fiction.Headless Horseman: Washington Irving's 1820 ghost in The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, possibly just Brom Bones in disguise.
Ghosts in fiction.King Boo: The ghost king of the Mario games, a bigger, crowned version of the Boos who hide when you look at them.
Ghosts in fiction.Blinky: The red Pac-Man ghost. In the original arcade game, the four ghosts each hunt in a different way.
Ghosts in fiction.Peeves: Hogwarts's poltergeist, a prankster ghost who is famously absent from the Harry Potter movies.
Ghosts in fiction.Bloody Baron: Slytherin's ghost, covered in silvery blood and wearing chains as penance for killing the Grey Lady.
Ghosts in fiction.Dracula: A trap: Dracula is a vampire, a physical undead body with fangs, not a bodiless ghost.
Ghosts in fiction.Frankenstein: The monster is not a ghost, and the name Frankenstein belongs to the scientist who made it.
Ghosts in fiction.Count Orlok: The vampire of the 1922 film Nosferatu, so a physical monster and not a spirit.
Ghosts in fiction.Imhotep: The mummy of The Mummy series, a physical body brought back to life, not a ghost.
Ghosts in fiction.Wolfman: A man-wolf in the 1941 Universal film, played by Lon Chaney Jr. A living shapeshifter, not a spirit.
Ghosts in fiction.Gollum: A twisted, ring-obsessed creature of Middle-earth who lives in caves. Corrupted hobbit stock, not a ghost.
Ghosts in fiction.Dobby: Harry Potter's house-elf. Dobby is a living being who can be freed with a gift of a sock.
Ghosts in fiction.Jack Skellington: The Pumpkin King is a skeleton, not a ghost, in The Nightmare Before Christmas.
Ghosts in fiction.Lurch: The Addams Family's towering butler is human, though his groan and dry delivery are creepy.
Ghosts in fiction.Igor: A hunchbacked assistant, a staple of mad scientist films. Alive, with a pulse, so not a ghost.
Ghosts in fiction.Uncle Fester: The bald Addams Family uncle is living, famous for lighting a bulb in his mouth, not a ghost.
Ghosts in fiction.Medusa: A Greek Gorgon with snakes for hair whose gaze turned people to stone. A living monster, not a ghost.

Silent ways to communicate.Braille: Created by Louis Braille in 1824 when he was a teenager, a tactile code of raised dots read by touch.
Silent ways to communicate.Morse code: Tapped out as dots and dashes; the first public message in 1844 was 'What hath God wrought'.
Silent ways to communicate.Sign language: Not universal: American and British Sign Language are unrelated, and each has its own grammar and vocabulary.
Silent ways to communicate.Semaphore: Flags held in set positions stand for letters, a method long used by navies for silent ship-to-ship messages.
Silent ways to communicate.Smoke signals: Used by Native peoples and also in ancient China, where towers along the Great Wall sent warnings by smoke.
Silent ways to communicate.Flag signals: Ships use letter flags with meanings; the 'A' flag, Alpha, means a diver is down, so keep clear.
Silent ways to communicate.Lip reading: Many sounds look identical on the lips, so lip readers rely heavily on context to understand speech.
Silent ways to communicate.Pantomime: From the Greek for 'imitator'; Marcel Marceau made silent acting famous around the world.
Silent ways to communicate.Charades: Began as a 19th-century French parlor game where players acted out words syllable by syllable.
Silent ways to communicate.Handwriting: The earliest writing dates back over 5,000 years to Mesopotamia, so silent communication has an ancient pedigree.
Silent ways to communicate.Texting: The first text message was sent in December 1992 and read 'Merry Christmas'.
Silent ways to communicate.Fingerspelling: Hand shapes stand for the letters of the alphabet, used within sign languages mainly to spell out names.
Silent ways to communicate.Phone call: Alexander Graham Bell's first words in 1876 were reportedly 'Mr. Watson, come here'; it is voice, not silence.
Silent ways to communicate.Radio show: A broadcast of voices and music, not silent, which was a mass medium from the 1920s.
Silent ways to communicate.Megaphone: It simply amplifies the voice, so it is definitely not silent; the name comes from Greek for 'big sound'.
Silent ways to communicate.Podcast: The name blends iPod and broadcast, coined around 2004, but it is entirely voice-based, not silent.
Silent ways to communicate.Yodeling: Rapid switches between chest and head voice developed in the Alps for calling across valleys, so very loud.
Silent ways to communicate.Intercom: An intercom lets rooms or buildings talk by voice, so there is no silence here.
Silent ways to communicate.Walkie-talkie: Developed by Motorola in World War II for soldiers, a voice radio that is far from silent.
Silent ways to communicate.Voicemail: A phone message that stores spoken words, and many people now avoid listening to them, so it is not silent.
Silent ways to communicate.Karaoke: Japanese for 'empty orchestra', and about as far from silent as music gets.
Silent ways to communicate.Lecture: From Latin 'to read', because medieval teachers read texts aloud, so it is anything but silent.
Silent ways to communicate.Audiobook: Early 'Talking Books' for blind veterans appeared in the 1930s, with spoken words that are never silent.
Silent ways to communicate.Town crier: Announced news by voice, often with a bell and the cry 'Oyez', so a loud job, not a silent one.
